title: Hot and Cold Bands on Earth
subtitle: A globe, climate bands, and city cards
coreQuestion: Why are some places hot and some places cold?
learningGoals: Know that Earth has different climate bands.
Understand that places near the equator are often hotter and places near the poles are often colder.
Connect city location, climate, clothing, plants, and daily life.
misconceptions: Weather is about the same everywhere.
All faraway places are simply hot or cold.
A flat map is the whole story of Earth.

hero.title: Hot and Cold Bands on Earth
hero.lead: Earth is a big ball. Different places receive sunlight in different ways, so life feels different there.
hero.sceneExplanation: The main visual is a child-friendly globe. Soft horizontal bands show tropical, temperate, and cold regions. City cards sit in different areas; tapping a city shows weather impressions, clothing ideas, and everyday life scenes.
hero.childPrompt: Tap a city and guess: should we bring shorts, an umbrella, or a thick coat?
hero.parentPrompt: The goal is not exact climate classification. Build the chain: Earth is a sphere — sunlight is different — places feel different — life changes.

classificationGroups.name: Tropical area
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Near the equator, many places are warm or hot all year.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Use ‘near the equator’ to build spatial sense; no latitude numbers needed.
classificationGroups.misconception: Tropical does not mean sunny every day; it may rain a lot too.

classificationGroups.name: Warm and humid area
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Some places are not in the hottest tropics, but they are warm for much of the year.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Shenzhen can be a familiar anchor city.
classificationGroups.misconception: The child’s own city is not the weather standard for the whole world.

classificationGroups.name: Temperate area
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Temperate places often have clearer seasons: warm times and cold times.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Beijing and London can show that temperate cities still differ.
classificationGroups.misconception: Temperate does not mean always warm.

classificationGroups.name: Dry hot area
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Some places are hot but have little rain, so the land feels dry.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Cairo can introduce hot and dry, not the same as tropical rainforest.
classificationGroups.misconception: Hot places are not always humid.

classificationGroups.name: Cold area
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Far north or far south places are often colder and need warmer clothes.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Use snow, wind, and coats as everyday anchors.
classificationGroups.misconception: Cold places still have cities and daily life.

representativeObjects.name: Singapore
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Singapore is near the equator. It is often hot and rainy.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking tropical places are only sunny.

representativeObjects.name: Shenzhen
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Shenzhen is warm for much of the year, with hot summers and lots of rain.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking all cities feel like your city.

representativeObjects.name: Beijing
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Beijing has more obvious seasons: hot summer and cold winter.
representativeObjects.visualHint: short sleeves in summer, thick coat in winter

representativeObjects.name: London
representativeObjects.childExplanation: London is also temperate, often mild, with a strong rainy-day impression.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking cities in the same band are exactly the same.

representativeObjects.name: Cairo
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Cairo is near dry hot desert environments, with strong sunshine in the day.
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking all hot places are rainforests.

representativeObjects.name: Reykjavik
representativeObjects.childExplanation: Reykjavik is far north and often feels cold.
representativeObjects.visualHint: thick coat, cold wind, northern city
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Thinking cold places have no city life.

mechanism.title: Why are some places hot and some cold?

steps.childExplanation: Earth is not a flat sheet. It is a big ball.
Sunlight reaches different places in different ways. Near the equator it is more direct; near the poles it is more slanted.
steps.parentNote: A flashlight and ball demonstration works well.

steps.childExplanation: That is why Earth has hot, mild, and cold regions.
steps.parentNote: This is a simplified first model.

steps.childExplanation: Climate affects clothes, plants, animals, and homes.
steps.parentNote: Connect climate back to everyday life.

comparePairs.title: Singapore vs Reykjavik
comparePairs.childConclusion: A city’s place on Earth affects how hot or cold it feels.

comparePairs.title: Shenzhen vs Beijing
comparePairs.childConclusion: Even in one country, cities can have different climates.

comparePairs.title: Hot wet vs Hot dry
comparePairs.childConclusion: Hot places can still be very different.

clickTasks.title: Which city is closest to the equator?
clickTasks.prompt: Look for the city in the hottest band.

wrongHints.beijing: Beijing is in a temperate area, not the hottest band.
wrongHints.reykjavik: Reykjavik is far north and much colder.

clickTasks.successCopy: Correct! Singapore is close to the equator and often feels hot and humid.

clickTasks.title: Find: which cities may need a thick coat?
clickTasks.successCopy: Good observation! Colder places often need warmer clothes.
clickTasks.wrongHint: Think about which cities are farther from the hot band.

clickTasks.title: Why is it often hotter near the equator?

options.label: Because the equator is much closer to the Sun
Because sunlight hits more directly there
Because there are more cities there

wrongHints.closer-sun: The key is not that it is much closer. It is how sunlight hits the surface.
wrongHints.more-cities: Cities do not create the main climate bands.

clickTasks.successCopy: Right! More direct sunlight helps make the equator warmer.

clickTasks.title: How climate bands form
clickTasks.prompt: Tap the idea chain in order.

options.label: People, plants, and animals live differently

clickTasks.successCopy: You built the climate idea chain.
clickTasks.wrongHint: Start with the shape of Earth: it is a ball.

speakTemplates: ____ is located more toward ____, so it often feels ____.
If I visit ____, I may bring ____ because ____.
Today I found out: hot places can be ____ or ____.
parentTips: Do not focus on exact climate categories yet. Build spatial understanding first.
Use a flashlight and ball to show sunlight angle.
Ask life-based questions: what would you wear, what plants might you see, what houses might help?
acceptanceCriteria: The child understands different places on Earth can feel different.
The child can match at least three cities to rough climate impressions.
The child can say that places near the equator are often warmer.
